text.tspan: Where coupling comes from, and what you can do about it
For any coupling you meet: where does it come from, who can change it, and
Integration strength: what one side must know about the other. From
strong to weak: intrusive (private internals), functional (business logic),
model (the internal model), contract (an interface built for integration).
Distance: how far apart the coupled parts are: same method, module,
service, team, company. Ownership counts as distance.
Volatility: how often the upstream side changes. Core subdomains
change often, supporting and generic ones rarely.
Balance does not last: new features add strength, splits and
reorganisations add distance, a new business strategy changes
The same rules hold from methods to services.
BALANCE = (STRENGTH XOR DISTANCE) OR NOT VOLATILITY
Stable coupling, e.g. writing straight into a bought product's database that hardly changes.
the business (process owners, product management); legislators,
regulators and standards bodies when the rule is given

Who owns each decision? Who should decide it,

tspan.tspan: What can we do, and what does it cost?

text.tspan: Weaken what crosses the boundary: an interface built for
integration instead of your internal model; public integration
events instead of your internal ones; an anti-corruption layer; one
Shorten the distance: move what changes together into one
Isolate volatility: put the part that changes often behind a stable
Change the decision outside the code: the business clarifies the
rule or the process; management changes team boundaries or how
Absorb it: contract tests, release coordination, an extra check
where it hurts. These costs never stop.
